title: Of sumptuary laws
paragraphs: The way our laws try to regulate idle and wasteful spending on food and clothing seems to me quite the opposite of what they intend. The right way would be to breed a contempt in men for silks and gold as vain, frivolous, and useless; whereas we, in fact, enhance their honour and price tag, which is hardly the way to put people off them. To pass a law that nobody but princes can eat turbot, or wear velvet and gold lace, and to forbid these things to ordinary people — what is that but to bring them into greater esteem, and set everyone all the more on edge to eat and wear them? Let kings leave off these emblems of grandeur; they have plenty of others. Such excesses are more excusable in anyone else than in a prince. We can learn from the example of several nations better ways to mark out social rank (which I do think is necessary in a state) without nourishing this kind of corruption and obvious nuisance. It is strange how quickly and easily custom in these indifferent things establishes itself and becomes authority. We had hardly been wearing plain cloth a year, in keeping with the court's mourning for Henry II, before silks had already fallen into such contempt with everyone that a man dressed in silk was automatically taken for a tradesman; silks were split between the doctors and surgeons, and although almost everyone else went about in the same kind of dress, there was nevertheless, in one thing or another, sufficient distinction of social rank. How suddenly do greasy chamois and linen doublets become the fashion in our armies, while all neatness and richness of dress fall into contempt? Let kings just take the lead and begin to give up this expense, and within a month the thing will be done throughout the kingdom, without edict or ordinance; we shall all follow. It ought rather to be proclaimed, on the contrary, that nobody should wear scarlet or goldsmith's work but courtesans and acrobats.

Zeleucus by the same kind of stratagem reclaimed the corrupted manners of the Locrians. His laws were that no freewoman should be allowed any more than one maid in attendance, unless she was drunk; nor was to go out of the city by night, wear gold jewellery, or go in an embroidered robe, unless she was a professed and public prostitute; that, apart from bravos, no man was to wear a gold ring, nor be seen in one of those effeminate robes woven in the city of Miletus. By these humiliating exceptions he cleverly diverted his citizens from superfluities and pernicious pleasures, and it was a project of great utility — attracting them to their duty and obedience through honour and ambition.
Our kings can do whatever they please in such external reformations; their own inclination, in this case, stands for law:
["Whatever princes themselves do, they seem to be prescribing." — Quintilian, Declam., 3.]

Whatever is done at court passes for a rule throughout the rest of France. Let the courtiers turn on those abominable breeches that show off so much of what should be concealed; these huge-bellied doublets that make us look like I-don't-know-what and are so unfit for wearing under arms; these long, effeminate locks of hair; this foolish custom of kissing what we hand to our equals, and our hands when we greet them, a ceremony in former times reserved only for princes. Let them not permit a gentleman to appear in any place of respect without his sword, with his clothes unbuttoned and uncinched, as if he had just come from the privy; and that, contrary to the custom of our forefathers and the particular privilege of the nobles of this kingdom, we stand a long time bareheaded before them in whatever place, and the same to a hundred others — so many tiercels and quartelets of kings we have these days, and other vicious innovations: the courtiers will see them all vanish at once and fall out of favour. These are, it's true, only superficial errors; but they are of bad omen, and enough to inform us that the whole structure is cracked and tottering when we see the rough-cast on our walls split and crumble.

Plato in his Laws considers nothing more pestilent in the consequences for his city than to give young men licence to introduce any change in their clothes, gestures, dances, songs, and exercises, from one form to another — shifting from this to that, chasing after novelties, and applauding the inventors; through which manners are corrupted and the old institutions come to be despised and held in contempt. In everything except what is evil, change is to be feared; even the change of seasons, winds, foods, and humours. And no laws are in their true credit but such as God has given so long a continuance to that no one knows their beginning, or that there ever was any other.
